`36-58`: **Comment indicates expectation but test doesn't validate it.** Line 55 states "we expect the string method to be more precise" but there's no assertion to verify this. Consider adding assertions to validate precision requirements. --- `59-85`: **Precision metrics calculated but not validated.** The test calculates useful precision metrics (absolute precision loss, relative error) but doesn't assert they're within acceptable bounds. --- `86-112`: **High precision test lacks validation.** Similar to other tests, this calculates precision loss but doesn't assert requirements. --- `113-141`: **Edge case test lacks validation.** Edge cases are particularly important to validate. Consider asserting precision requirements for these critical scenarios. --- `12-35`: **Tests document but don't validate precision requirements.** The test prints precision differences but doesn't assert any requirements. This means the test will pass even if significant precision loss occurs. If precision loss is acceptable for this use case, consider: 1. Asserting an acceptable tolerance threshold, or 2. Marking these as informational/manual tests with a clear comment explaining they're for documentation only
🔎 Suggested improvement to assert precision requirements If you want to enforce that precision loss is within acceptable bounds: ```diff # Document precision loss, if any if string_result != double_result: print(f"Precision difference for {py_decimal}:") print(f" String method: {string_result}") print(f" Double method: {double_result}") print(f" Difference: {abs(string_result - double_result)}") + # Assert precision loss is within acceptable bounds + relative_error = abs(string_result - double_result) / abs(string_result) if string_result != 0 else 0 + assert relative_error < 1e-10, f"Precision loss too high: {relative_error}" ``` Alternatively, if these are purely informational, add a docstring note and consider using `pytest.mark.manual` or similar.
